clinicalPearls: Autosomal recessive disorder caused by loss-of-function variants in KCNJ10, encoding the inwardly rectifying potassium channel Kir4.1
Remember the acronyms: EAST (Epilepsy, Ataxia, Sensorineural deafness, Tubulopathy) and SeSAME (Seizures, Sensorineural deafness, Ataxia, Mental retardation, Electrolyte imbalance)
Seizures usually begin in infancy, followed by a non-progressive cerebellar ataxia and developmental delay
The renal phenotype resembles a Gitelman-like salt-losing tubulopathy with hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis, hypomagnesaemia, and hypocalciuria
Sensorineural hearing loss reflects Kir4.1 expression in the stria vascularis of the inner ear
Management is supportive: anticonvulsants for seizures, potassium and magnesium supplementation, and rehabilitative support for deafness and ataxia
Consider the diagnosis in any child with early seizures plus an unexplained salt-losing tubulopathy, and confirm with KCNJ10 sequencing
reference.pathophysiology: Kir4.1 is an inwardly rectifying potassium channel expressed in glial cells of the brain, the stria vascularis of the cochlea, and the basolateral membrane of the distal convoluted tubule. In the kidney it recycles potassium to maintain the activity of the basolateral sodium-potassium ATPase, so that loss of Kir4.1 function impairs sodium chloride reabsorption in the distal tubule, producing a Gitelman-like picture of renal salt wasting, hypokalaemic alkalosis, hypomagnesaemia, and reduced urinary calcium. Loss of the channel in astrocytes disturbs potassium buffering and glutamate handling, giving rise to epilepsy and cerebellar dysfunction, while its absence in the inner ear disrupts the endocochlear potential and causes sensorineural deafness.
additionalDifferentials: Mitochondrial cytopathies with deafness and tubulopathy
Congenital sensorineural deafness syndromes (e.g. Pendred, Usher)
additionalInvestigations: Serum electrolytes including magnesium demonstrating hypokalaemia and hypomagnesaemia
Venous blood gas showing metabolic alkalosis
Spot urinary calcium-to-creatinine ratio showing hypocalciuria
Audiometry and brainstem auditory evoked responses for sensorineural loss
MRI brain and electroencephalography for seizures and cerebellar signs
KCNJ10 gene sequencing to confirm the diagnosis
redFlags: Poorly controlled or status epilepticus in infancy
Severe symptomatic hypokalaemia risking cardiac arrhythmia
Profound hypomagnesaemia precipitating tetany or seizures
Failure to thrive and developmental regression
reference.prognosis: Seizures and electrolyte disturbances are usually manageable with treatment and the ataxia is typically non-progressive, but neurodevelopmental delay and permanent sensorineural deafness contribute to long-term disability; renal salt wasting generally does not progress to renal failure.
pitfalls: Labelling the tubulopathy as isolated Gitelman syndrome and overlooking the neurological features
Attributing the seizures to a primary epilepsy without checking electrolytes
Under-recognising hypomagnesaemia as a contributor to seizure threshold
Missing early hearing loss that would benefit from amplification
management: Control the infantile-onset seizures with antiseizure medication
Correct the Gitelman-like salt-losing tubulopathy with oral potassium and magnesium supplementation
Add potassium-sparing or aldosterone-antagonist therapy and sodium supplementation as needed for renal salt wasting and hypokalaemic alkalosis
Provide rehabilitative support for cerebellar ataxia and developmental delay through physiotherapy, occupational therapy and educational support
Offer hearing rehabilitation for sensorineural deafness, including hearing aids or cochlear implantation
Monitor serum electrolytes, magnesium and renal function over the long term
Offer genetic counselling and family testing given autosomal recessive KCNJ10 inheritance
Coordinate multidisciplinary care across nephrology, neurology, audiology and clinical genetics
